articles.title: The RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro is a rugged phone with a Go Pro-style action cam
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro is a curious mash-up that combines two products into one, and doesn’t make a total mess of that attempt. However, the action camera isn’t a replacement for a GoPro, even if it might be remarkably useful.
Pros
- +Extremely rugged
- +Detachable action camera
- +Powerful SoC and plenty of RAM
- +Action camera is rated to 5M underwater
Cons
- -Odd-shaped phone
- -Only 2.7k video on action cam
- -Limited range for action cam control
- -Kickstarter launch
Why you can trust TechRadar
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: 30-second review
Launched at the Berlin IFA this year, the RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro fuses two well-known products into something genuinely new.
In this case, those elements are the rugged Android smartphone and the small action camera. In this design, the two can be separated, giving you a rugged phone that can spawn an action camera, the Xsnap Go, whenever you need one.
But ignoring that aspect for a moment, what does the Xsnap 7 Pro offer for those who just need a rugged Android phone? As rugged designs go, this one doesn’t have a massive battery, but it does have a decent processor in the Dimensity 9400, and with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, the specifications are at the higher end of this scale.
Also, even if you don’t use the detachable camera, the built-in cameras are decent and capable of good results. But the party trick is the tiny square camera that can be removed from its slot in the back of the phone, which doubles as a charger, and then remotely controlled to capture images and video.
It connects via the platform's WiFi hotspot, and all captures are stored in the 64GB of internal camera storage before later transfer to the phone. The maximum video resolution is 2.7 K, but it supports anti-shake and the option to flatten the barrel distortion the fisheye lens creates.
This camera isn’t a direct competitor to any camera GoPro recently made, the DJI Osmo Nano, or Insta360 Go Ultra. However, it’s included in the price, and it could be useful for anyone who needs to be in a location where using the camera built into the phone isn’t convenient.
This design probably isn’t the best rugged phone, since the action camera slightly compromises it, but if you need a solid, powerful phone with a detachable camera, this is it.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: price and availability
- How much does it cost? $999
- When is it out? Available now
- Where can you get it? Launched on Kickstarter on the 7th of September 2026
I don’t follow why so many Chinese device makers do this, but RugOne initially launched this phone on Kickstarter. The supposed purpose of that platform is to get funding for a concept to turn it into a finished product, but since I had the review hardware almost before the Kickstarter launched, it appears to be entirely a marketing exercise.
When the Kickstarter opened for pledges on 7 September 2026 with an early bird price of $899 (€799), Wider retail availability is planned for October 2026, at $999 in the United States and €1,099.99 across Europe.
As with any Kickstarter campaign, backers are funding a pledge rather than making a conventional purchase. Delivery estimates, warranty terms and final specifications can all shift between a campaign page and a shipped product, and this is worth stating plainly in the published review rather than leaving it as an implication.
That said, the phone and camera do exist, but I can’t give you more definitive timescales or pricing, which isn’t helpful.
If the phone alone was $999 at launch, I’d be inclined to think it was overpriced. But with the camera included, that’s a whole different calculation based on what you think the camera is worth.
A DJI Osmo Nano Standard Combo (64GB) is roughly $390 with 64GB onboard, but that’s a camera that’s capable of 4K at 60fps and a 200-minute battery life.
If I optimistically value the Xsnap Go camera at half that value, then $800 still seems a little steep for the phone. But there is some convenience in having the camera housed in the phone and charged from it.
Sadly, I don’t recall seeing any other products with this arrangement, so the choice is either this, a phone, or a phone-and-action-camera combo.
- Value score: 3.5/5
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Specs
| Item | Spec | 
| CPU: | MediaTek Dimensity 8400 (MT6899Z/ZA), octa-core up to 3.25GHz | 
| GPU: | ARM Mali-G720 MC7 | 
| NPU: | MediaTek NPU 880 | 
| RAM: | 12GB | 
| Storage: | 512GB UFS 4.0 | 
| Screen: | 6.67-inch AMOLED | 
| Resolution: | 1220 x 2712 (1.5K), 120Hz, 445ppi, 1700 nits peak | 
| Screen Protection: | Corning Gorilla Glass Victus | 
| SIM: | 2x Nano SIM + eSIM (two of three can be used) | 
| Weight: | 477g | 
| Dimensions: | 172.5 x 83.4 x 28mm | 
| Rugged Spec: | IP68 IP69K dust/water resistant (up to 2m for 30 minutes), MIL-STD-810H Certification | 
| Rear cameras: | 50MP Main Camera + 64 MP Night Vision Camera | 
| Front camera: | 32MP | 
| Detachable camera: | 2.7K@30fps, 1440p@30fps, 1080p@30fps, 64GB storage | 
| Networking: | 5G. WiFi 6E, Bluetooth 5.4 | 
| Audio: | 3.5mm audio jack for headphones | 
| OS: | Android 16 (updates promised) | 
| Battery: | 9,200mAh (Max 45W wired, 50W wireless, 10W reverse) | 
| Colours: | Sand Dune, Black | 
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Design
- Curious structure
- Detachable Xsnap Go camera
- Lots of accessories
There is something about the Xsnap 7 Pro that smacks of the kind of exercises students do when they're aiming to become industrial designers. In that, taking two disparate devices and fusing them into one can be an interesting challenge.
The problem the people behind this phone didn’t solve was how to house a camera that’s 25mm deep without making it implausibly thick at one end.
We’re all used to the camera cluster being raised to provide extra depth for the optics and sensors, but this design takes that a whole extra level.
Curiously, RugOne quotes the thickness as 19.1mm, but I measured it, and 28mm seems more accurate. The upshot is that it goes in a pocket more easily upside down, but getting past the camera bulge might be difficult unless you have huge pockets.
Removing the camera doesn’t make it any thinner.
The mechanism for detaching the Xsnap Go camera is straightforward yet quite annoying. To release the camera, press the button below it and then, gripping the edge of the lens cover, pull it out. I’m making this sound simpler than it is, because the camera is held in place not only by the latch the button operates but also by magnets. If you loosen your grip at all when removing it, the camera will shoot back into its home in an instant.
The magnets are there because the rear of the camera has contact pads that connect it to the phone for charging, and for them to work, they need to be flush with the opposing pins on the bottom of the recess.
Putting it back in is much easier, as once the magnets grab, it automatically locates.
The space the removable camera occupies forces the rear integrated camera sensors to the left, where they are vertically stacked.
Away from that area, the back is entirely flat and has a backlit RugOne logo running across it that is called the Aura Pulse, which can be set to animate for an incoming call or a notification. Unfortunately, the LEDs behind it are too dim to be useful, as I had a hard time telling whether it was working even in a dimly lit room.
Potentially more useful, the flat part of the underside does support wireless charging. However, because a significant amount of weight is in the raised area, I couldn’t balance it on my Ugreen charger without it toppling over.
Most of the rest of this design uses the standard playbook for rugged phones, with the power and volume rockers on the right, along with one custom button and another customisable button on the left intended for Walkie-talkie use. The SIM card slot is next to the USB-C port, and the phone is IP68 rated for water resistance even if that port doesn’t have a rubber plug.
The only notable feature at the top end is an IR blaster, which lets the Xsnap 7 Pro act as a remote control if you need it.
The 6.67in AMOLED panel runs at 1220 x 2712, which RugOne markets as 1.5K, with a 120Hz refresh rate and a claimed 1700 nits of peak brightness. Corning Gorilla Glass Victus sits on top, a sensible choice for a phone that will spend time in pockets, tool bags and glove boxes.
On paper, this puts the Xsnap 7 Pro's screen ahead of many rugged phones, which often settle for lower resolution or dimmer panels to save cost. Brightness claims from any manufacturer are difficult to counter, but this one is one of the brighter ones I’ve tested when measured directly under daylight conditions against other devices.
One thing I liked about this exceptionally bright and colourful display is that it has an under-screen fingerprint sensor, which makes it much easier to use for left-handers.
Overall, from the outside, this looks like a dozen ruggedised designs Ulefone (RugOne) has made, except for the swelling needed to accommodate the removable camera. I’d be more critical of those design choices if I could imagine a way of including it without it creating the ergonomic compromises it plainly created. But I can’t think of how this might have been better, so it is what it is.
Design score: 3.5/5
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Hardware
- MediaTek Dimensity 8400
- UFS 4.0 storage
- USB 3.2 Gen 1 port
- 9300mAh battery
The underlying platform used here is the MediaTek Dimensity 8400, an octa-core chip built on Arm Cortex-A725 cores and paired with an Arm Mali-G720 MC7 GPU. It is a genuinely modern mid-to-upper-tier platform, backed here by 12GB of RAM and 512GB of UFS 4.0 storage, with the option to borrow further RAM from storage through Android's virtual memory feature.
If you see claims of 24GB of RAM, that’s marketing people getting overly excited about that feature and trying to claim virtual memory is real RAM.
For me, the important takeaway is the UFS 4.0 storage. One of the things I noticed almost immediately about this device is how quickly it downloads and installs applications. Read and write speeds are a major factor in that speed, along with the processing power of the Dimensity 8400.
Another unexpected feature RugOne included is that the USB-C port isn’t the same as what most phone makers include. While it has the physical housing of a modern USB-C port, most phones only have it wired to the USB 2.0 standard, capping the file transfer speed at around 40Mb/s.
On this device, the port is actually wired as USB 3.2 Gen 1, which enables much faster file delivery. This is only possible because the UFS 4.0 storage can keep pace, something that a phone with UFS 2.2 or 3.0 storage wouldn’t be able to offer.
A 9,300mAh cell is a reasonable capacity for any phone, rugged or otherwise, and RugOne claims up to seven days of typical use. That’s probably a significant oversell, since my testing suggests that a couple of days can eat through that capacity if the battery use isn’t managed.
Charging is handled over 45W wired PD or 50W wireless, with 10W reverse wireless charging thrown in for topping up earbuds or accessories. However, one additional draw on the battery power is the action camera. If you use the camera, once returned to the phone, it immediately starts to charge from the battery until its internal battery is fully charged.
Therefore, if you run low on power, I’d recommend not re-docking the camera.
Docked back onto the phone, RugOne claims up to 20 full recharges of the module from the phone's battery, extending total shooting time to a claimed 800 minutes across a full charge cycle of the handset.
The kit includes an independent charger for the camera, so you can keep it fully charged with a power pack.
- Hardware score: 4/5
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Cameras
- 50MP and 64MP on the rear
- 32MP on the front
- Detachable Xsnap Go action cam
- Four cameras in total
The RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro has four cameras:
Rear cameras: 50MP Samsung GN9, 64MP OmniVision OV64B Night vision
Front camera: 32MP GalaxyCore GC32E1
Detachable camera: OmniVision 5MP OV-OS05A10
The primary camera on the Xsnap 7 Pro is the classic Samsung GN9 sensor, a 50MP OIS design with an f/1.88 aperture and 84° FOV optics. If this were the only sensor on this phone, it would be reasonable, since it’s a solid design that can take great pictures, especially in good lighting conditions.
In my examples, I accidentally left HDR mode on, so the colours are excessively punchy, but it will take better, more colour-balanced images if you leave it off. The GN9’s weakness is that it has no zoom optics, so you're limited to basic digital zoom.
The other weakness of most Samsung primary sensors is that they tend to get grainy when the light level drops. Thankfully, if you want sharp images in complete darkness, then the 64MP OmniVision OV64B is a great option. And, as long as the subject is within the IR illumination, it will be captured precisely.
The 32MP Samsung GC32E1, f/2.45 sensor is probably overkill for a FaceTime camera, but it's in so many phones these days that it's almost becoming a de facto standard.
But none of these cameras is why you would consider this phone, so let’s get to the detachable Xsnap Go action module, which uses the OV-OS05A10 sensor, a 133° FOV, f/2.4, 14mm equivalent.
Before we get into the details of this device, I want to talk about some of the mechanics of using this device, and how it doesn’t always work the way you might want it to.
For starters, you don’t use this camera through the camera app; instead, it uses its own dedicated Xsnap Go app, which will only talk to the detachable camera if certain phone settings are configured.
One requirement is a WiFi hotspot, so you can’t use it while the camera is active and also be logged into a local WiFi access point. You also need to remember to disable this when you are done, as the app won’t disable it when it exits.
With all settings configured, a link to the camera is established, whether the module is mounted on the phone or detached from it.
Which begs the question: how far can the phone and camera still talk? Not very far. I estimated the limit at about 30 ft if any structure is involved, and maybe 50 ft outdoors. One issue I ran into is that if the phone and camera disconnect while recording, the app can't easily re-establish the connection, and at least once I had to reboot the phone to get them to talk again.
You can use the camera's single button to take photos or record video without the app, but you won't know if it's run out of internal storage without the phone connected.
Via the app, you can select basic video recording, slow motion, time-lapse, interval photo and single still image capture. The 5MP sensor's best resolution is 2.7K, while the Samsung sensor on the phone offers 4K. The camera has 64GB of storage that isn't expandable, and you must instruct the device via the app to copy the captures to the phone's storage.
It offers various motion and distortion compensation options, and you can manually tweak exposure settings or use HDR. It’s clearly not up to the primary sensor's capabilities, but you can detach it and place it away from the phone for another perspective.
That could be incredibly useful for someone working, for example, on a vehicle engine who needs to be behind the steering wheel but still see what’s happening in the engine bay.
In my testing, I did some motion-compensated video and time-lapse, and the results were decent. The only issue I noticed, and some dedicated action cameras suffer with this too, is that if the exposure changes during a time-lapse, the camera can’t adjust for the new lighting conditions.
The run time of my time-lapse was 40 minutes and 30 seconds, half a minute more than RugOne claims for the battery life on the detachable camera. This runtime might have been longer if RugOne made better-considered accessories. The phone includes a small charging dock and a tripod mount accessory for the detachable camera.
Had these been one item, and not two, a power bank might have been able to keep the camera running for longer recordings. Unfortunately, they are separate and not designed to work together, as the camera can only be attached to one of them.
That said, the detachable camera is something unique about this design, and even with some notable limitations, it can be extremely useful.

RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Performance
| Phone |  | RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro | Oukitel WP500 Ultra | 
| SoC |  | MediaTek Dimensity 8400 | MediaTek Dimensity 8300 | 
| GPU |  | ARM Mali-G720 MC7 | ARM Mali-G615 MC6 | 
| NPU |  | MediaTek NPU 880 | MediaTek NPU 580 | 
| Memory |  | 12GB/512GB | 12GB/1TB | 
| Weight |  | 477g | 414.3g | 
| Battery |  | 9200 | 10000 | 
| Geekbench | Single | 1396 | 1239 | 
|  | Multi | 4789 | 3525 | 
|  | OpenCL | 7678 | 7196 | 
|  | Vulkan | 8513 | 8171 | 
| PCMark | 3.0 Score | 16075 | 15219 | 
|  | Battery | 23h 33m (17%) | 22h 37m (19%) | 
| Charge 30 | % | 28 | 42 | 
| Passmark | Score | 14225 | 18554 | 
|  | CPU | 11068 | 8748 | 
| 3DMark | Slingshot OGL | Maxed Out | Maxed Out | 
|  | Slingshot Ex. OGL | Maxed Out | Maxed Out | 
|  | Slingshot Ex. Vulkan | Maxed Out | Maxed Out | 
|  | Wildlife | Maxed Out | 7958 | 
| Row 20 - Cell 0 | Nomad Lite | 1305 | 953 | 
The Xsnap 7 Pro has a few good things, and one that isn’t so encouraging.
For comparison, I’ve used the Oukitel WP500 Ultra, a premium design that uses the slightly less impressive Dimensity 9300, and not the 9400 that the Xsnap 7 Pro sports.
Overall, in most tests, the Dimensity 9400 provides about another 10% of performance, and the ARM Mali-G720 MC7 is also a significant uplift.
It’s annoying that 3DMark is mostly overpowered by both these platforms, but the Nomad Lite test shows how the ARM Mali-G720 MC7 delivers when combined with the UFS 4.0 storage.
And that would be the whole story, if it wasn’t for the battery test.
Is the downside of the UFS 4.0 storage that it consumes more power? It certainly doesn’t seem that way, because with slightly less battery, the Xsnap 7 Pro lasted even longer than the WP500 Ultra.
I believe a contributing factor is the OLED display on this phone. My methodology for the battery benchmark is to reduce screen brightness to about 120 nits. And the OLED is so much brighter than a typical VA panel that its brightness setting is around 20%, not 40% or more.
What’s harder to tell is whether having the detachable camera connected and charging from the phone also has a significant impact. It’s nice that you can recharge the camera without needing the charging base, but does that come with a catch? Maybe, but you can always remove the camera from the phone and charge it separately.
- Performance score: 4/5
RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro: Final verdict
I have mixed feelings about this design for a few reasons. But before we get to the caveats, I need to call out the lovely build quality that RugOne-branded hardware is rocking, which is generally excellent. This phone feels exceptionally well made and able to take more than a few light knocks. That makes it suitable for anyone who works outdoors or in harsh environments.
The base platform is also elegantly powerful, making the experience responsive and useful in a wide range of situations. If you occasionally game or use VR, this phone has enough power to do it smoothly.
The standard camera installation is workmanlike and can deliver good results. However, the detachable Xsnap Go camera isn’t quite at the same level, and you need to configure it optimally to get the best results. If 2.7K resolution video and a 40-minute battery life are enough for your needs, this could be the phone for you, but it doesn’t embarrass any dedicated action cameras currently on the market.
If you work alone but need to be in two places at once to observe events, this solution might work for you, as long as you can work with the limited camera runtime.
The camera's caveat is that it makes the phone harder to pocket, and it could drain the internal battery when you don’t want it moving to the camera.
But minor points aside, this is still a unique offering that some professions might find invaluable.
Should I buy a RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro?
| RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro Score Card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | Kickstarter launch, but the specifications weren’t going to make this a cheap phone | 3.5/5 | 
| Design | Including the camera has made this phone an odd shape | 3.5/5 | 
| Hardware | Powerful SoC and UFS 4.4 storage combine well | 4/5 | 
| Cameras | Good primary camera sensor and night vision, but only 2.7K on the Xsnap Go | 4/5 | 
| Performance | Lots of SoC power and plenty of storage, but battery performance could be better | 4/5 | 
| Overall | A unique offering, but it might cost more than a phone and an older GoPro | 4/5 | 
Buy it if...
You need remote viewing
Being able to detach the camera and view that in a different location could be incredibly useful in numerous occupations. The range is limited, but being able to capture video and still images while live viewing could be a game changer.
You need a powerful phone
The Dimensity 9400 in the Xsnap 7 Pro is a powerful modern SoC with enough performance for most applications. Using 512GB of UFS 4.0 storage and a proper USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 port, this device is perfect for those who push their equipment hard.
Don't buy it if...
You already have an action camera
The Xsnap Go is a modest action camera with only 2.7K resolution that doesn’t offer the same feature set as a GoPro or Insta360. If you have one of these, you can do roughly the same things, but typically at 4K resolution or better.
Battery life is critical
The weakness of this design is battery life, as the performance of the phone reduces run time and recharging the Xsnap Go camera also takes its toll. If you want a phone that will still be operational after a week in the wilderness, then this isn’t it.
For more ruggedized devices, we've reviewed the best rugged tablets, the best rugged laptops, and the best rugged hard drives
Mark is an expert on 3D printers, drones and phones. He also covers storage, including SSDs, NAS drives and portable hard drives. He started writing in 1986 and has contributed to MicroMart, PC Format, 3D World, among others.

articles.title: Como abrir a área de transferência do PC para ver o histórico do CTRL C • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Como abrir a área de transferência do PC para ver o histórico do CTRL C
A área de transferência do Windows permite gerenciar o histórico do CTRL C, acessando até 25 conteúdos copiados anteriormente no PC
A área de transferência do Windows otimiza a produtividade ao salvar tudo o que você envia para a memória com o tradicional CTRL C. Esse recurso inteligente vai muito além de uma simples cópia única, permitindo gerenciar blocos de texto e imagens de forma prática.
Para abrir a área de transferência do Windows, você deve primeiro ativar a função nas configurações do sistema e, depois, pressionar o atalho Windows + V. Esse comando simples revela um painel completo com todos os conteúdos copiados recentemente para você reutilizar quando quiser.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog te mostra como ativar e ver a área de transferência do PC Windows.
Como acessar o histórico da área de transferência do Windows
- Abra as configurações do Windows pressionando o atalho Windows + I no teclado.
- Vá em “Sistema” e, depois, selecione o menu “Área de transferência”.
- Ative a chave ao lado da opção “Histórico da área de transferência” para permitir que o sistema memorize os itens copiados.
- Após ativar a função, utilize o atalho da área de transferência, Windows + V, para abrir o painel flutuante e ver o histórico de CTRL C do PC.
Dá para limpar o histórico da área de transferência do PC?
Sim, é possível apagar o histórico de copiar e colar ao abrir a área de transferência do Windows. Na janela flutuante, você pode remover um item específico ou clicar em “Limpar todos” os dados de uma só vez.
Essa ação elimina as informações salvas na memória temporária local e na nuvem, sendo fundamental para proteger dados sensíveis contra acessos indesejados.
Qual o limite da área de transferência do PC?
A área de transferência do Windows armazena até 25 itens recentes, aceitando formatos de texto, código HTML e imagem bitmap de até 4 MB por arquivo. Ao atingir esse limite, o sistema descarta automaticamente o registro mais antigo para abrir espaço para o novo conteúdo copiado.
É possível ver o histórico da área de transferência do Chromebook ou do Mac?
Sim, dá para ver o que foi copiado anteriormente tanto no Chromebook quanto no Mac. Cada sistema utiliza comandos e recursos próprios para gerenciar esse histórico.
- Chromebook: pressione as teclas Busca + V (ou Launcher + V) para abrir o painel de transferência e visualizar os itens copiados na sessão;
- Mac: abra a busca digitando Command + Espaço e, em seguida, digite Command + 4 para acessar o histórico do Spotlight nas versões recentes do macOS.
O celular também guarda o histórico de copiar e colar?
Sim, a área de transferência do celular fica integrada ao teclado virtual dos aparelhos Android. O atalho permite ver o que foi copiado anteriormente, além de gerenciar quais conteúdos ficam salvos na memória RAM do smartphone.
No iPhone, o sistema iOS armazena apenas o último item copiado por padrão, visando à segurança dos usuários. Caso queira consultar um histórico mais completo, é necessário utilizar aplicativos de terceiros.

articles.title: Agentic security strategy faces a shrinking breach window- SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Agentic security strategy faces a shrinking breach window
An agentic security strategy must account for software that can act on legitimate instructions in unexpected ways. Agents can use credentials, call tools and choose their own routes toward a goal, expanding the paths security teams need to watch.
The risk arises even when no one instructs an agent to cause harm. Traditional controls such as least privilege and defense in depth become more consequential as agents gain authority, according to Zulfikar Ramzan (pictured), former chief technology officer and chief digital officer of RSA Security USA LLC.
“[Agents] can even choose among many different paths towards accomplishing a task,” Ramzan said. “And that … is what’s gotten really interesting in the last few weeks even, where a legitimate objective can still lead an agent down a path that’s unintended, making … the types of controls we’ve talked about for decades in this industry all the more important.”
Ramzan talked with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle’s “AI Cyberattacks Are Escalating: How to Secure Your Data Now” event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed agent privileges, the narrowing window between intrusions and breaches and how security teams can adapt their response. (* Disclosure below.)
An agentic security strategy starts with agent identity
Before setting limits, organizations need to know which agents exist, whose identities they use and which systems they can reach. Broad access to tools complicates applying longstanding security principles to tasks that unfold across several steps, according to Ramzan.
“Least privilege does become harder when agents need broad access to different tools and capabilities,” he said. “If you give an action to an agent around a multi-step task, we’ve got to now think about things like strong authorization and monitoring in that context.”
Ramzan argued that organizations need protection throughout an attack, including the point where sensitive data resides. He sees protecting data at its source as a final line of defense if an attacker gets past earlier controls.
“Intrusion is that first step in the attack. It’s that first foothold, so to speak,” Ramzan said. “But it’s not the goal of the attacker. That breach, which is the actual material compromise of an asset, that is what ultimately the attacker is after.”
Shortening the path from detection to recovery
The time available to intervene after an intrusion is narrowing as attackers use AI to find and exploit weaknesses, Ramzan noted. Defenders need to speed up verification and remediation while still checking the effects of patches before deployment.
“AI can create an asymmetry between that machine-speed discovery and the exploitation of what you find and human-speed triage,” he said. “That’s testing, approvals, patching and recovery. The reality is that we’re not going to be able to keep up with system-level speed.”
Security teams know which assets and operations matter most to their business, giving them a way to prioritize their defenses. That knowledge should shape where they invest, according to Ramzan.
“Continuously learn from every incident that occurs,” he said. “Look at those near misses where you got away with it, but maybe you shouldn’t have. Take that input, take that insight [and] feed it back into your security program on a regular basis.”
Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE Research’s coverage of Oracle’s “AI Cyberattacks Are Escalating: How to Secure Your Data Now” event:

articles.title: Meta ofrecerá a las empresas agentes de IA de Muse para automatizar tareas y optimizar sus negocios
articles.text:
Meta anunció el lanzamiento de Meta Enterprise Platform, una nueva plataforma con la que ofrecerá sus modelos de inteligencia artificial, agentes y herramientas de programación a empresas y desarrolladores. El servicio permitirá incorporar tecnologías como Muse, Meta Business Agent, Muse API y Muse Code para automatizar tareas, desarrollar aplicaciones y optimizar las operaciones de los negocios.
Para liderar esta nueva iniciativa, la compañía contrató a Chirantan “CJ” Desai, quien hasta ahora se desempeñaba como director ejecutivo de MongoDB. El ejecutivo reportará directamente a Mark Zuckerberg y asumirá el cargo de director de plataforma empresarial, desde el que estará a cargo de convertir las tecnologías de inteligencia artificial de Meta en productos destinados al mercado corporativo.
PUBLICIDAD
Meta llevará sus agentes de IA al mercado empresarial
La nueva plataforma reunirá diferentes herramientas de inteligencia artificial de Meta en un servicio dirigido a organizaciones que buscan incorporar estas tecnologías a sus operaciones. Entre ellas destaca Muse, un agente capaz de ejecutar tareas mediante instrucciones de los usuarios, además de Meta Business Agent, Muse API y Muse Code.
La propuesta de la compañía consiste en ofrecer a las empresas acceso a sus modelos y agentes de inteligencia artificial para que puedan utilizarlos en sus propios negocios. Esto incluye desde la automatización de determinadas actividades hasta el desarrollo de aplicaciones y la integración de nuevas funciones en sus servicios.
PUBLICIDAD
Mark Zuckerberg explicó que la plataforma aprovechará los modelos avanzados, los agentes y la infraestructura tecnológica de Meta, así como la experiencia acumulada en su trabajo con distintas empresas. El objetivo inicial será poner ese conjunto de herramientas a disposición de organizaciones y desarrolladores para facilitar la creación de soluciones basadas en inteligencia artificial.
La iniciativa también representa un cambio en la estrategia comercial de la compañía, que busca ampliar el alcance de sus tecnologías más allá de sus propias aplicaciones y convertirlas en servicios para clientes corporativos.
Muse y Meta Business Agent, entre las herramientas disponibles
Uno de los componentes centrales de la nueva plataforma será Muse, el agente de inteligencia artificial que Meta presentó a principios de septiembre. Esta herramienta está diseñada para realizar distintas tareas a partir de las instrucciones de los usuarios, como comprar productos, reservar viajes, enviar correos electrónicos y efectuar pagos.
PUBLICIDAD
Aunque inicialmente fue concebido como un asistente personal, su tecnología también forma parte de la estrategia de Meta para ofrecer soluciones de inteligencia artificial a las empresas.
La plataforma incluirá, además, Meta Business Agent, una herramienta orientada al entorno corporativo, así como Muse API y Muse Code, que permitirán integrar las tecnologías de la compañía y desarrollar soluciones de programación.
Con esta oferta, Meta busca que las empresas puedan incorporar sus agentes y modelos de inteligencia artificial a diferentes procesos, sin limitarse a utilizar los asistentes disponibles en sus aplicaciones.
El fichaje del CEO de MongoDB para liderar el nuevo negocio
Para dirigir esta iniciativa, Meta contrató a Chirantan “CJ” Desai, un ejecutivo con experiencia en el sector tecnológico que asumió la dirección de MongoDB hace menos de un año. Antes de llegar a esa compañía, estuvo al frente de las áreas de producto e ingeniería de Cloudflare y trabajó durante casi ocho años en ServiceNow, donde ocupó los cargos de presidente y director de operaciones.
PUBLICIDAD
Desai reemplazará en MongoDB a Dev Ittycheria, quien asumirá temporalmente la dirección ejecutiva mientras la empresa busca un sustituto permanente. Su salida provocó una caída del 18 % en las acciones de la compañía durante la sesión matutina del lunes.
Pese a esta reacción del mercado, la firma de análisis Piper Sandler consideró que MongoDB mantiene una posición estratégica favorable y calificó de exagerada la caída de sus acciones.
En Meta, Desai tendrá la responsabilidad de transformar las tecnologías de inteligencia artificial de la compañía en productos y servicios que puedan utilizar otras organizaciones. Su nombramiento se produce en un momento en el que la empresa busca ampliar sus fuentes de ingresos y aprovechar la demanda empresarial de soluciones basadas en inteligencia artificial.
PUBLICIDAD
Con Meta Enterprise Platform, la compañía pretende trasladar sus avances en inteligencia artificial al entorno corporativo y ofrecer a las empresas herramientas para automatizar tareas, desarrollar aplicaciones e incorporar agentes inteligentes a sus operaciones.

articles.title: El problema del coche eléctrico en China ya no es venderlo, sino qué hacer con sus baterías cuando mueren
articles.text:
China ya lleva un buen tiempo en esto de los coches eléctricos, por lo que el país ahora está entrando en una fase en la que tiene que pensar qué hacer con todas las baterías de sus vehículos que van poco a poco degradándose. Para ello va a contar con dos recetas principales: regulación e innovación en sus procesos de reciclaje.
Mucha batería suelta. Las autoridades chinas prevén que las baterías usadas superen el millón de toneladas al año para 2030, según cuenta Xinhua. Se trata de un fuerte aumento con respecto a las aproximadamente 200.000 toneladas retiradas en 2020, cifra que citaba la televisión estatal CCTV en un informe de 2021 y que para 2025 proyectaba unas 780.000 toneladas en total.
Como habrás podido imaginar, las baterías no están hechas para durar para siempre, y eso es uno de los grandes problemas del vehículo eléctrico, pues una vez que su capacidad cae a alrededor del 80 %, generalmente no se consideran aptas para propulsar un automóvil. Además, el problema no es solo ambiental, pues una batería que no se encuentre en buen estado o no se gestione de forma correcta conlleva a riesgo de incendio o puede filtrar materiales peligrosos. Éstas además contienen metales valiosos que China preferiría mantener en su propia cadena de suministro.
En cifras. Según el Ministerio de Industria y Tecnología de la Información de China (MIIT), tanto la producción como las ventas de vehículos de nuevas energías (NEV, que incluyen coches eléctricos de batería e híbridos enchufables) superaron los 16 millones de unidades en 2025, más de la mitad de todas las ventas de vehículos nuevos en el país. Pekín quiere que esa cuota alcance el 70 % para 2030, según comparte CnEVPost. Y claro, cada uno de esos coches necesitará en un futuro que se gestione su batería.
Qué está haciendo Pekín. En enero, el MIIT y otros cinco departamentos publicaron medidas provisionales sobre el reciclaje de baterías que entraron en vigor el 1 de abril. Su idea central es mantener la batería vinculada a su coche hasta el final. Según las normas, un vehículo eléctrico desguazado sin su batería de tracción será clasificado como un vehículo incompleto. El objetivo es evitar que las baterías se filtren a canales no controlados, como talleres de terceros o vertederos ilegales. Las normas no cubren los modelos de intercambio de baterías, por lo que el MIIT afirma que todavía está estudiando cómo gestionarlos.
Cómo funcionará. El gobierno afirma que cada batería de tracción obtendrá una identidad digital, y una plataforma nacional de trazabilidad la seguirá desde la producción hasta las ventas, reparación, desguace y reciclaje. Además, los fabricantes de baterías deben hacerse cargo de las baterías que produzcan o importen para el mercado chino, excepto las vendidas directamente a los fabricantes de automóviles, según comparten desde CnEVPost.
Por otro lado, según la normativa, los fabricantes e importadores deben abrir estaciones de servicio de reciclaje en las regiones donde vendan, tal y como cuentan desde CarNewsChina. También deben aceptar baterías retiradas de empresas de alquiler (leasing), intercambio de baterías y reparación, y no pueden rechazarlas. Además, solo las empresas legalmente autorizadas pueden llevar a cabo la reutilización y el reciclaje a gran escala.
UN VISTAZO A...
Entre líneas. Desde CarNewsChina cuentan que el mercado de reciclaje de baterías de China alcanzó los 558.000 millones de yuanes (unos 73.300 millones de euros) el año pasado, y que Brunp Recycling, filial de CATL, afirma gestionar el 50,4 % de las baterías de vehículos eléctricos del país, con una capacidad de 120.000 toneladas. El mismo medio señalaba que algunas empresas chinas pueden recuperar el 96,5 % del litio y el 99,6 % del níquel, cobalto y manganeso.
A pesar de que exista tecnología capaz de recuperar esos materiales, hay un desafío mayor que consiste en llevar las baterías viejas a las instalaciones adecuadas y evitar que la industria tome atajos. CarNewsChina señala que el sector lleva mucho tiempo luchando contra la falta de infraestructuras, los riesgos de incendio y el costoso desmantelamiento causado por diseños de baterías no estandarizados.
Y ahora qué. El nuevo plan de la industria de baterías para el periodo 2026-2030, publicado por el MIIT esta semana, amplía el enfoque. Requiere que las empresas establezcan sistemas de recogida de baterías usadas en proporción a sus ventas y las anima a crear capacidad de reciclaje en los principales mercados de exportación donde las condiciones lo permitan, según comparte CnEVPost.
También propone un sistema de pasaporte de baterías y el reconocimiento mutuo de los datos de huella de carbono, lo que sería importante para los fabricantes de automóviles chinos que venden en el extranjero. En el ámbito tecnológico, el plan aspira al uso a gran escala de baterías de estado totalmente sólido para 2030, y a baterías de litio capaces de realizar 15.000 ciclos de carga y descarga, lo que frenaría el ritmo de las retiradas.

articles.title: Placer une pièce de monnaie sur son routeur Wi-Fi : pourquoi et à quoi ça sert
articles.text:
Placer une pièce de monnaie sur son routeur Wi-Fi : pourquoi et à quoi ça sert
L'astuce fait le tour des réseaux sociaux : poser une pièce, ou un bout d'aluminium, sur sa box internet améliorerait la connexion. La réalité physique est tout autre. Non seulement le métal ne renforce pas le signal, mais il peut le dégrader et faire surchauffer l'appareil. Voici ce qui marche vraiment.
C'est une astuce de grand-mère version numérique qui revient régulièrement sur YouTube : poser délicatement une simple pièce de deux euros sur le dessus de sa box internet permettrait d'obtenir enfin un réseau fluide et sans coupures. Entre démonstrations convaincantes et commentaires enthousiastes, la promesse est séduisante. Le geste est si simple et gratuit qu'on serait tenté de l'essayer sur-le-champ. C'est pourtant là que se niche le piège de ces recettes miracles qui circulent en ligne.
Une croyance séduisante mais sans fondement
L'idée paraît presque logique. Le métal réfléchit les ondes, alors une pièce posée sur la box redirigerait le signal Wi-Fi et étendrait sa portée. C'est sur ce raisonnement que repose l'astuce, largement relayée. Sauf qu'aucune preuve technique ne la soutient, et les spécialistes des télécoms sont unanimes pour la réfuter. Poser un objet métallique sur ou contre un routeur n'améliore rien, et peut même aggraver la situation.
Si certains utilisateurs jurent avoir constaté un mieux, il s'agit au mieux d'un effet placebo, au pire d'une coïncidence avec un simple redémarrage de la box au moment de la manipulation. La vérité est que l'amélioration du Wi-Fi ne passe jamais par un gadget posé sur le boîtier, mais par le placement de l'appareil et par ses réglages. La pièce, elle, ne fait qu'ajouter un problème là où il n'y en avait pas.
Pourquoi le métal nuit au signal, et à l'appareil
La physique explique clairement pourquoi cette astuce se retourne contre l'utilisateur. Les antennes d'une box sont des circuits calibrés au millimètre pour émettre sur des fréquences précises. Approcher un objet métallique conducteur perturbe leur environnement immédiat et décale leur fréquence de résonance, un phénomène que les ingénieurs appellent le désaccordage d'antenne. Résultat, une partie de l'énergie n'est plus rayonnée vers la pièce, mais réfléchie vers les circuits internes de la box, avec une perte d'efficacité qui peut dépasser 50 %.
Le métal déforme aussi le diagramme de rayonnement, ce halo en forme d'anneau selon lequel la box diffuse normalement son signal. Au lieu d'une couverture homogène, on crée des zones d'ombre et des réflexions incontrôlées. À cela s'ajoute un risque matériel : un objet posé sur le boîtier bloque les grilles de ventilation. La box chauffe, déclenche une sécurité qui bride ses performances, et souffre à la longue d'une usure prématurée. En cherchant à gagner quelques mégabits, on abîme donc l'appareil.
Les gestes qui améliorent vraiment le Wi-Fi
Bonne nouvelle, les vraies solutions sont tout aussi simples et, elles, réellement efficaces. La première tient au placement. Installez la box en hauteur, à environ 1,5 mètre du sol, et au centre du logement. Posée par terre ou cachée dans un meuble, elle perd jusqu'à 30 % de sa portée et risque la surchauffe. Éloignez-la des masses métalliques, des murs épais, mais aussi des perturbateurs comme le four à micro-ondes, les téléphones sans fil ou même un aquarium, l'eau absorbant fortement les ondes.
Asus ZenWiFi BT8
Côté réglages, quelques ajustements changent tout. Réservez la bande 5 GHz aux usages intensifs proches de la box, streaming ou visio, et gardez la 2,4 GHz, qui traverse mieux les murs, pour les objets connectés éloignés. Une application d'analyse réseau permet de repérer un canal moins encombré par le voisinage. Reliez en câble Ethernet vos appareils fixes, ordinateur de bureau ou console, pour libérer les ondes. Et pensez à redémarrer la box de temps en temps, puis à maintenir son logiciel à jour. Pour les grands logements, un système de répéteurs ou un kit CPL fera le reste. Autant de gestes qui, contrairement à la pièce de monnaie, reposent sur la science plutôt que sur la rumeur.

articles.title: Google conteste en justice deux ordres européens sur Android et le partage des recherches
articles.text:
Alphabet conteste devant la justice européenne deux décisions prises dans le cadre du DMA. Bruxelles veut donner aux assistants IA concurrents un accès plus profond à Android et ouvrir une partie des données de Search. Le groupe estime que ces obligations vont trop loin en matière de sécurité et de vie privée.
Le géant de Mountain View ne compte pas appliquer sans discuter les nouvelles règles européennes imposées à Android et à son moteur de recherche. Le groupe a saisi le Tribunal de l’Union européenne contre deux décisions adoptées par la Commission le 16 juillet dernier dans le cadre du Digital Markets Act. Il ne s’agit pas d’amendes, mais de prescriptions très concrètes sur la manière dont Google doit ouvrir ses services à ses concurrents. Les recours ont été déposés le 28 septembre et ne suspendent pas, à eux seuls, les obligations contestées.
Android devra laisser davantage de place aux rivaux de Gemini
La première bataille se joue directement dans le smartphone. Bruxelles estime que les assistants concurrents de Gemini doivent pouvoir accéder aux mêmes fonctions essentielles d’Android que celui de Google.
Onze briques sont concernées, de l’activation vocale à l’accès au contexte affiché à l’écran, en passant par la possibilité d’agir dans d’autres applications ou de travailler en arrière-plan. L’objectif est qu’un assistant installé par l’utilisateur puisse, par exemple, rédiger un e-mail, ajouter un produit à une liste ou automatiser une tâche avec un niveau d’intégration comparable à Gemini.
L’essentiel de ces changements doit arriver avec Android 18, au plus tard le 1er août prochain. Seule l’activation vocale simultanée de plusieurs assistants pourra attendre Android 19, au plus tard le 1er août 2028.
La filiale d’Alphabet estime que cette ouverture risque d’affaiblir certaines protections du système. La Commission répond que l’accès restera soumis au consentement de l’utilisateur et que des conditions particulières pourront être imposées pour les fonctions les plus sensibles. Le Tribunal devra désormais déterminer si l’UE pouvait imposer ces accès et leurs garde-fous dans les conditions retenues.
Google Search devra partager une partie de ce qui fait sa force
Le second recours touche à une matière encore plus sensible : les données issues des recherches des utilisateurs. Le DMA impose à Google de fournir aux moteurs concurrents (y compris certains services d’IA intégrant une fonction de recherche) des données anonymisées sur les requêtes, clics, consultations et classements pour qu’ils puissent améliorer leurs propres résultats. L’algorithme de Google, lui, ne doit pas être transmis.
La Commission prévoit plusieurs filtres : suppression des requêtes contenant des termes rares ou présentant une longueur inhabituelle, généralisation de la localisation et audits réguliers des entreprises souhaitant accéder au jeu de données.
Elle assure également qu’aucune information liée au compte ni aucun historique individuel de recherche ne seront transmis. Google devra avoir finalisé les données anonymisées en novembre, puis son offre tarifaire d’ici à janvier 2027.
Pour Mountain View, cela ne suffit pas. Oliver Bethell, son responsable de la concurrence, estime que des recherches particulièrement intimes pourraient malgré tout être partagées avec une anonymisation insuffisante.
Bruxelles affirme au contraire avoir conçu son dispositif avec des spécialistes de la protection des données. Celui-ci permet par ailleurs d’écarter les entreprises présentant des risques sérieux.
Pour les utilisateurs, rien ne change donc immédiatement. Mais derrière cette bataille juridique se joue une question beaucoup plus concrète : jusqu’où peut-on obliger Google à ouvrir les avantages accumulés par Android et Search sans ouvrir, avec eux, une nouvelle porte sur nos données ?

articles.title: ATK Launches Blazing Sky Phantom: 44 g Carbon Fiber Wireless Gaming Mouse for $100-120
articles.text:
Tuesday, September 29th 2026
	
	
	
	
ATK Launches Blazing Sky Phantom: 44 g Carbon Fiber Wireless Gaming Mouse for $100-120
ATK has officially launched the Blazing Sky Phantom, a new wireless, carbon fiber composite gaming mouse that is promises a lightweight shell, flagship internals, and a reasonable price—at least compared to big gaming brands, like Razer and Logitech. ATK claims that the Blazing Sky Phantom weighs in at 44 g, although it has had to use honeycomb cutouts on the back of the shell in order to achieve this weight. The Blazing Sky Phantom is available on ATK's website for $99.98 during its pre-order period, after which it will increase to $119.98. Unlike most other carbon fiber mice, the Phantom is available in four different colors: Eon (Black) Prime (White), Verge (Blue), and Dune (Sand). 
The mouse shape is the typical symmetrical shape reminiscent of something like a Razer Viper V4 Pro, but with a few notable changes. For starters, the ATK is notably smaller, measuring in at 119.7 × 62.5 × 37.3 mm, compared to the V4 Pro's 127.1 × 63.9 × 39.9 mm, and potentially making it a better fit for a variety of grip types. It also has an updated Nano coating, which is meant to give gamers better grip during tense moments. The side buttons on the ATK Blazing Sky Phantom also appear to be located further forward compared to the Razer. Internally, the ATK Blazing Sky Phantom features the new PixArt PAW 3955 Master sensor combined with a Nordic 54LM20 MCU, giving it an 8 kHz polling rate in both wired and 2.4 GHz modes and a peak sensitivity of 50,000 DPI. The brand claims that the mouse has a 0.174 ms of latency, although it's never specified whether this is motion latency or click latency.The ATK Phantom's mouse switches are Omron Optical switches, and the scroll wheel uses a Raesha Optical encoder, making the whole thing a lot more resistant to wear and tear. ATK has put a 300 mAh battery inside the Blazing Sky Phantom, which it claims can deliver up to 200 hours of use at 1 kHz polling. Increasing that to 4 kHz or 8 kHz will dramatically reduce battery life. The mouse also ships with two dongles: The Gem 8K Dongle and the Nano 8K Dongle.

articles.title: Bug do Google fez milhares de apps para iPhone travarem • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Bug do Google fez milhares de apps para iPhone travarem
Falha no Google Analytics for Firebase enviou dados incorretos a aplicativos para iOS. Correção foi feita nos servidores e não exige atualização dos apps.
Uma falha em um serviço do Google fez milhares de aplicativos travarem em iPhones. Embora o problema tenha afetado dispositivos da Apple, a causa estava no Google Analytics for Firebase, ferramenta usada por desenvolvedores, e não no iOS.
Desenvolvedores discutiram o problema no GitHub nesta terça-feira (29/09): o serviço do Google enviou dados formatados incorretamente aos aplicativos e, ao tentar processar essas informações na inicialização, alguns apps fechavam menos de um segundo depois.
Um dos desenvolvedores do Google respondeu aos comentários e afirmou que a empresa já aplicou uma correção. Segundo ele, os desenvolvedores não precisam atualizar o Firebase nem publicar novas versões dos aplicativos para solucionar o problema.
O Google Analytics for Firebase serve para coletar métricas de uso e interação dentro dos aplicativos. O primeiro relato no repositório oficial descreveu uma elevação repentina no número de travamentos. Em apenas 18 minutos, um desenvolvedor registrou 56 falhas entre 56 usuários.
A investigação apontou que os travamentos começavam logo depois que o SDK recebia uma resposta dos servidores do Google. O aplicativo tentava processar os dados recebidos, mas encontrava uma informação inválida e era encerrado.
O Google confirmou mais tarde que a causa era o pacote de dados formatado incorretamente. Segundo o Android Authority, milhares de aplicativos que utilizam o Firebase foram afetados. Em alguns casos, desenvolvedores relataram números de travamentos mais de 5 mil vezes acima do normal.
A falha foi comunicada por volta das 21h41 (horário de Brasília) desta segunda-feira (28/09). A companhia informou que concluiu a distribuição da correção às 23h52 do mesmo dia. Como a solução foi feita do lado dos servidores, desenvolvedores não precisam publicar novas versões dos aplicativos.
Informações armazenadas em cache poderiam continuar causando travamentos por até quatro horas após a distribuição da correção. Segundo o Google, esses casos restantes deveriam desaparecer por volta das 3h52 de hoje, conforme os dados antigos fossem substituídos.

articles.title: Oracle CISO puts humans at the center of AI security governance - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Oracle CISO puts humans at the center of AI security governance
As enterprises face AI-driven cyberattacks, AI security governance must control autonomous systems that can reach data, connect applications and act on users’ behalf. That makes human accountability a core security requirement.
Traditional controls remain necessary, but security teams must also understand the data flows and processes agents create. People, therefore, need a new role in supervising consequential actions, according to Brennan Baybeck (pictured), senior vice president and chief information security officer of Oracle Customer Success at Oracle Corp.
“Humans have never been more critical to help control these robots, as we call them,” he said. “We used to say humans are the weakest link. But now what I’m saying is that robots are the most powerful and potentially dangerous link, and humans are now an essential link.”
Baybeck talked with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle’s “AI Cyberattacks Are Escalating: How to Secure Your Data Now” event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed human oversight of AI agents, AI security governance and the shared responsibility between customers and technology providers. (* Disclosure below.)
AI security governance returns to first principles
That oversight must rest on basic controls, including least privilege, authorization, network segmentation and monitoring. Yet Baybeck sees three recurring gaps as organizations put AI into production.
“There’s definitely some patterns that we’re seeing, and there’s three of them that I want to highlight,” he said. “The first one is a lack of a solid foundational governance program for AI. The second one is not having the security basics in place to start with, especially in their Oracle ecosystems. And then not understanding the shared security responsibility model when it comes to AI services with service providers.”
The shared model assigns security duties to both providers and customers. At the same time, AI can help security teams produce policies, standards and assessment tools faster, Baybeck added.
“Security professionals can leverage AI and actually create a governance program, associated policies, standards, processes and best practices in a matter of hours,” he said. “There is no excuse anymore of why we don’t have a governance program in place at any company because you can literally use AI services to create that and have a very well-thought-out and deployable governance program.”

articles.title: Snapmaker launches its U1 3D printer that will appeal to creators, hobbyists and newcomers - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Leading technology company Snapmaker has launched its new U1 3D printer in Australia which is aimed at a broader range of customers, including creators, educators, hobbyists, and small businesses.
The Snapmaker U1 is a 4-toolhead 3D printer and can make multi-colour and multi-material 3D prints faster and more efficiently.
The printer was first launched through Kickstarter last year where it received support from 20,680 backers and raised $US20.6 million.
The attraction of the new unit is its ease of use which will make it easier for newcomers to 3D printing to get started.
Conventional multi-colour systems load different filaments through the same nozzle but the U1 has four independent tool heads, with each colour or material loaded on its own filament path.
So when a print requires a different colour or material, the unit swaps the entire tool head instead of unloading and reloading filament through the same nozzle.
Snapmaker says a typical tool change takes about 5 seconds.
Another benefit of its tool changer architecture is the substantial reduction in waste associated with multi-colour printing.
Snapmaker says the U1 produce up to 85 per cent less filament waste than shared-nozzle filament-switching 3D printers.
Apart from different coloured filament, the Snapmaker U1 also allows users to use different types of filament for their prints.
New types of filament include rigid and flexible filaments or dedicated support materials so you can produce more complex functional parts while reducing the need for manual material changes.
The UI can automatically calibrate the multiple toolheads, load filament, and monitor the print.
There is even a small camera built in so users can connect via the companion app to see the progress of their work.
The Snapmaker U1 has a build volume at 270 x 270 x 270 mm which is a generous amount of space for your 3D prints.
“Making digital creation more accessible has always been central to Snapmaker,” says Sheila She, Head of Global Go-to-Market at Snapmaker.
“We designed the U1 to make multi-colour and multi-material printing faster, cleaner, and easier to use, while reducing the material waste commonly associated with filament changes.
“We’re excited for Australian customers to discover and experience tool changing 3D printing.”
The Snapmaker U1 is available now for pre-order through JB Hi-Fi and Harvey Norman at the discounted price of $1,299.
The Snapmaker U1 will go on sale on October 15 and will be priced at $1,399.

articles.title: Impresoras antiguas antigua dejarían de funcionar con este cambio que hará Microsoft en Windows 11
articles.text:
Si tienes una impresora antigua que funciona sin problemas, no habría motivo para cambiarla. Pero Microsoft prepara una transformación en Windows 11 que podría dejarla fuera de servicio en el futuro.
Durante 25 años, los controladores desarrollados por los fabricantes fueron la pieza central de la impresión en Windows. Ahora la compañía avanza hacia un modelo basado en estándares abiertos, con el objetivo declarado de reducir los riesgos de seguridad que ese esquema arrastraba desde hace décadas.
PUBLICIDAD
Qué cambia en el sistema de impresión de Windows
Hasta ahora, cada marca gestionaba su propio software. Comprar una impresora de un fabricante implicaba instalar y actualizar su controlador específico para que el equipo la reconociera.
Windows busca simplificar ese esquema con un sistema común de comunicación con los dispositivos, apoyado en estándares como IPP (Internet Printing Protocol), ya utilizado para conectar impresoras en red, y Mopria.
El repliegue del modelo anterior ya comenzó. Desde enero de 2026, los nuevos controladores de terceros dejaron de publicarse a través de Windows Update. Desde julio del mismo año, el sistema empezó a priorizar sus propios controladores cuando existe uno compatible disponible.
PUBLICIDAD
Qué es Windows Protected Print Mode, el punto de quiebre
El cambio más determinante llegará con Windows Protected Print Mode (WPP), una función que ya existe en Windows 11 pero que hoy resulta opcional. Cuando está activada, el sistema deja de aceptar controladores de terceros y utiliza en su lugar uno desarrollado por Microsoft, compatible con impresoras certificadas bajo el estándar Mopria.
Con este esquema, las impresoras compatibles se comunican mediante IPP, mientras que funciones adicionales como el grapado, los folletos o la gestión del tóner pasan a ejecutarse mediante aplicaciones aisladas, descargadas desde Microsoft Store, y no como parte del spooler del sistema.
Microsoft ya confirmó su intención de que Protected Print Mode se convierta en la configuración predeterminada de Windows 11, aunque todavía no fijó una fecha para ese cambio.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo afecta a las impresoras actuales y qué hacer
El cambio no implica que una impresora deje de funcionar de un día para otro. Si un modelo está instalado y opera con normalidad, seguirá haciéndolo mientras Protected Print Mode continúe como una opción y no como configuración predeterminada.
El problema aparecerá cuando Microsoft active WPP por defecto. En ese momento, los modelos que dependan exclusivamente de un controlador antiguo del fabricante, sin compatibilidad con IPP o Mopria, dejarán de ser reconocidos por el equipo.
Este escenario también reconfigura la gestión de flotas de impresoras en las empresas. En lugar de instalar y mantener controladores según la marca y el modelo, los administradores deberán verificar si cada dispositivo cumple con un estándar abierto.
PUBLICIDAD
Por el momento, la recomendación es continuar utilizando la impresora que ya funciona con normalidad. Sí conviene revisar la compatibilidad del modelo con IPP o Mopria: si el dispositivo depende de un controlador que el fabricante dejó de actualizar hace años, esa información resultará clave antes de que Windows adopte Protected Print Mode como estándar predeterminado.
Microsoft problemas en las actualizaciones de Windows 11
Microsoft confirmó que actualizaciones recientes de Windows 11 provocan pantallas negras al iniciar sesión, con bloqueos de escritorio y fallos del Explorador de Windows. El problema afecta principalmente a equipos de Azure Virtual Desktop con FSLogix, aunque también aparece en versiones 26H1, 25H2 y 24H2.
PUBLICIDAD
Como solución temporal, se puede reiniciar el proceso “explorer.exe” desde el Administrador de tareas. Para empresas, Microsoft habilitó la función Known Issue Rollback, con las políticas KB5124006 (26H1) y KB5124010 (25H2 y 24H2), que exigen reinicio tras aplicarse.
“Esta directiva de grupo deshabilitará el cambio que causa este problema hasta que se publique una solución”, indicó Microsoft. El incidente figura como “mitigado”, mientras la compañía trabaja en una corrección definitiva.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: 'Super svelte, super comfy and gloriously expansive': Technics' new over-ear headphones are very good indeed — here's why the EAH-A1000 could become class-leaders
articles.text:
Technics EAH-A1000 initial review: Technics' just updated its superb EAH-A800 headphones, and I got them in advance — here's my early verdict
'Super svelte, super comfy and gloriously expansive': our early review is in
- Technics has unveiled new EAH-A1000 flagship wireless headphones
- The company's famed Magnetic Fluid Driver is literally making the big time
- Owing to last-minute tweaks/firmware updates, my full review is incoming
Today sees a huge reveal in the world of wireless headphones. Not only because it's been well over four years since Technics' excellent EAH-A800 landed (promptly gaining a glowing 4.5-star review from this publication, if you'll only click that link), but because the same 'magnetic fluid' magic that made the Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds soar straight to the top of our best earbuds buying guide (where they sit prettily even now) has somehow been massively upscaled.
Technics' proprietary concoction that once facilitated more accurate motion within a tiny 10mm driver, squirrelled within an earbud, is now able to lubricate a 40mm drive unit in a headphone ear cup. And for those lucky enough to have heard what it did for earbuds (feel free to read my various odes to the EAH-AZ100 buds if you need proof of its prowess), that is huge.
Speaking of luck, I was invited to the company's elite facility in Tokyo to talk to the team, find out more about the Technics EAH-A1000, and try them before anyone else. Oh, it's not lost on me, don't worry. And here are my initial thoughts…
Greige, but make it elite level
I was not given a 'Platinum Greige' set to take home, but my black review sample is incredibly stylish and promotes no small sense of pride in ownership. See how it glistens against a Tokyo skyline!
At the big unveil, I ask the design team why the case, bijou and useful though it is, is not imprinted with a Technics logo? I'm directed to demure branding on the zipper and told: "Everything at Technics must either be engraved onto the metal or embroidered to the fabric of a product: we do not print." Quite.
Everything here has been optimized for what Technics' Group Manager Ellison Ferdinand calls "an uncompromising experience". During a talk with the design team I'm shown countless samples of potential top-plates for the ear cup: too shiny, too textured, too yellowy through the concentric grooves of the metal. This is meticulous attention to detail, and then some.
Back to that Magnetic Fluid Driver though, and to further enhance its performance the EAH-A1000 incorporates an SST (Symmetrical Surround Technology) Edge — yes, the same tech that's also used in Technics hi-fi flagship speakers. So, pure rigid carbon fiber diaphragm, with dome shape and cone shape ideas within it (think a dish with a slight raise in the center, rather than a regular cone), along with a redesigned acoustic control chamber, to manage airflow more precisely. The idea across the board is that by improving the drivers' pistonic movement, these design flourishes further minimize distortion (the enemy of accuracy and clarity). The EAH-A1000 also features a new 'Baffle Flat Structure' to reduce "uneven surfaces around the driver, limiting unwanted reflections".
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Stamina and so on? Of course: high-resolution audio playback via LDAC and USB Audio is on the menu plus up to 45 hours of continuous playback (without ANC and LDAC deployed, of course), and multipoint connectivity to up to three devices — which is still a perk unique to Technics' headphones and earbuds.
13 degrees doesn't sound like a lot, but to me it makes all the difference
The arms of the headphones have been thinned and refined since the EAH-A800, and I think it's a wise and beautiful solution. Upon slipping them over my head, they have remained supremely comfortable too (I'm around 60% through TechRadar's rigorous testing process), which I believe is due to the 13-degree angle of the ear cups, relative to the headband. This was implemented by the female Head of Design on this particular Technics release. Apparently, over 500 people tested them prior to landing on this design, and half were women. Bravo. (Women like music too.)
This missive is not to be taken as a full review. As mentioned, I'm only part-way through testing because, as is normal when trialing products not yet officially in the public domain, the EAH-A1000 are only just now running their final software version. As such, small tweaks have recently been implemented, and it would be premature of me to offer feedback on elements within these headphones in the run-up to their release that I can't be sure others will experience. That said, they are now official, and will be available to purchase as of tomorrow (September 30).
What I can tell you — aside from pricing, which is officially $449 / £399 / €449 (so around AU$750 as a ballpark figure) — is that so far, the sound quality is nothing short of superb. I do not write this lightly. I have toyed with the head-tracked spatial audio profile, optimized for Dolby Atmos, as well as the ANC, and while I'm impressed, watch this space for my final verdict. For now, know that the multi-function button/slider (to tweak volume and alter playback) is a better solution than controls via touch capacitive surfaces. And the circumaural distribution of sound is like that of a skilled pastry chef, creating a layered, tall, elegant croquembouche around my ears.
Essentially, they're super svelte, super comfy and gloriously expansive. Things are looking good…

Becky became Audio Editor at TechRadar in 2024, but joined the team in 2022 as Senior Staff Writer, focusing on all things hi-fi. Before this, she spent three years at What Hi-Fi? testing and reviewing everything from wallet-friendly wireless earbuds to huge high-end sound systems. Prior to gaining her MA in Journalism in 2018, Becky freelanced as an arts critic alongside a 22-year career as a professional dancer and aerialist – any love of dance starts with a love of music. Becky has previously contributed to Stuff, FourFourTwo and The Stage. When not writing, she can still be found throwing shapes in a dance studio, these days with varying degrees of success.

articles.title: OpenAI DevDay 2026 : quand et comment suivre la keynote ce soir, et ce qu'OpenAI pourrait dévoiler
articles.text:
OpenAI tient ce mardi 29 septembre son DevDay 2026, à San Francisco. La keynote de Sam Altman sera diffusée en direct à 19h00, heure française, et l'entreprise devrait annoncer plus de vingt lancements, dont peut-être Aeon, un agent IA très attendu.
Pendant que la France passera à l'apéritif tout à l'heure, la Californie sera en pleine matinée, suspendue à la keynote d'OpenAI, qui promet au moins une vingtaines de lancements en une seule journée, excusez du peu ! Le DevDay 2026, grand rendez-vous annuel des développeurs de la firme qui propulse ChatGPT, va avoir lieu du côté de Fort Mason, à San Francisco. Où regarder, à quelle heure exactement, et que peut-on raisonnablement espérer ? Voici l'essentiel à savoir, avant le lever de rideau.
OpenAI promet 20 lancements au DevDay 2026, voici comment suivre la keynote ce soir
La keynote d'ouverture, avec Sam Altman à l'affiche, sera retransmise en direct sur la page francophone d'OpenAI ici même. Le coup d'envoi de la conférence est fixé à 10h00, heure du Pacifique, soit 19h00 en France métropolitaine. Les plus distraits peuvent laisser leur prénom, leur nom et une adresse e-mail pour recevoir une alerte, sous forme de notification, une petite heure avant le début. Ça, c'est pour l'aspect pratique.
Ajoutons qu'outre la keynote, qui est le temps fort dont OpenAI annonce la diffusion en direct, auront lieu tout au long de la journée (donc de la soirée, pour les Français) des sessions techniques, des démonstrations et ateliers qui ont été pensés pour les développeurs présents sur place. À San Francisco d'ailleurs, le programme s'étirera jusqu'à une réception à 19h00, heure locale, soit 4h00 du matin chez nous. C'est donc a priori la keynote qu'il faudra suivre pour découvrir les annonces phares. Allez, passons au plus important, le contenu.
Aeon, l'agent IA qui pourrait être la star du jour
Officiellement, OpenAI s'en tient à ce fameux « 20+ », qui symbolise le nombre d'annonces attendues, sans dire s'il recouvre de vrais nouveaux produits ou un assortiment de fonctionnalités, de mises à jour et d'outils pour développeurs. On se souvient que l'an dernier, la cuvée alignait AgentKit, les apps dans ChatGPT ou Sora 2 dans l'API. GPT-6.1 Astra, lui, ne devrait pas être du voyage, car OpenAI a repoussé sa sortie, prévue en octobre, faute de satisfaire ses exigences de sécurité. L'appareil imaginé avec l'ancien designer d'Apple Jony Ive pourrait en revanche refaire parler de lui.
Le clou du spectacle devrait être Aeon. Selon les rumeurs relayées par la presse américaine ces dernières heures, OpenAI préparerait un agent actif en permanence, de ceux qui réservent un voyage, règlent des factures ou résilient un abonnement à votre place. Il reposerait sur le modèle GPT-6 Astra, dont OpenAI vante les prouesses. Peut-être les vrais débuts de l'ère de l'AGI, l'intelligence artificielle générale dont nous vous reparlerons plus longuement sur Clubic ces prochains mois, à n'en pas douter. En tout cas, petit détail révélateur : l'entreprise emploie Peter Steinberger, le père de l'agent open source OpenClaw.
Mine de rien, OpenAI part avec du retard. Lancé ce mois-ci, Muse, l'agent de Meta, s'est hissé en tête de l'App Store avec quelque 600 000 utilisateurs quotidiens aux États-Unis, même si des témoignages difficiles à vérifier l'accusent d'avoir divulgué une adresse sans permission. Gemini Spark, chez Google, se connecte déjà à une trentaine de services comme Uber ou Spotify. Instinct, joignable par iMessage, vient de lever un milliard de dollars. On n'oublie évidemment pas Anthropic, qui a sorti coup sur coup ou presque Claude Opus 5.5 et Sonnet 5.5. Avec une introduction en Bourse à l'horizon, OpenAI joue gros ce soir.

articles.title: Poner ventanas en las naves espaciales es clave para que los astronautas no se vuelvan locos. El problema es instalarlas
articles.text:
No valoramos la importancia de las ventanas, hasta que tenemos un baño sin ellas. O un piso de alquiler con ventanas a una tapia. O directamente un dormitorio sin ventanas. Pero si hay un lugar en el que las ventanas son más importantes todavía, este es el espacio. Sin embargo, durante mucho tiempo, no fueron una prioridad. En las misiones Mercury, las primeras estadounidenses en llevar humanos al espacio, los astronautas tuvieron que discutir con los ingenieros para lograr que incluyeran un ventanal en la cápsula. Desde entonces no ha hecho falta ninguna discusión, pero sí mucha investigación, ya que la ventana es importante, pero puede resultar muy peligrosa si no se construye con los materiales adecuados.
¿De qué sirve la experiencia si no la ves? En un artículo para Space, el periodista espacial Leonard David cuenta la anécdota de las misiones Mercury que se dio a conocer anteriormente en el libro “Elegidos para la gloria”, de Tom Wolfe. Al parecer, los ingenieros querían colocar ventanillas circulares muy pequeñas. De hecho, la cápsula de Alan Shepard, la primera Mercury que viajó al espacio, incluía ventanucos circulares de apenas 15 centímetros. Los astronautas pedían sustituir esto por un ventanal grande en la parte delantera, de manera que el piloto pudiese ver lo que había fuera en caso de tener que manejar manualmente la cápsula. No pedían tanto. ¿Cómo sería conducir un coche sin ventanillas?
Con el tiempo, las ventanas se empezaron a valorar mucho más, tanto por estas razones técnicas como por otros motivos. Estos incluyen los beneficios psicológicos de no ir, como señala David, encerrados en una caja, pero también los puramente experienciales. Poder ver la Tierra desde fuera es una experiencia única. Sin ventanas nada sería igual.
Cuantas más ventanas, mejor. Hoy en día, las ventanas son una parte indispensable de cualquier nave o instalación espacial. Cobran gran importancia en naves turísticas, como las de Virgin Galactic, SpaceX o Blue Origin, pero, en general, ayudan a disfrutar de la experiencia a cualquier astronauta. La propia Estación Espacial Internacional cuenta con una cúpula acristalada en la que los astronautas pasan mucho tiempo mirando hacia la Tierra.
Mejor evitar el vidrio. Para misiones de apenas un día como máximo, como las Mercury, no habría problema con usar vidrio. Sin embargo, este es un material que puede ser peligroso cuando la misión se alarga. Según declaraciones de Lynda Estes, responsable de transparencias de naves en el Centro Espacial Johnson de la NASA, el vidrio es frágil y se rompe con facilidad. Además, con el tiempo se pueden formar unas grietas microscópicas que crecen bajo carga, liberando pequeñísimos cristales que, bajo microgravedad, irían dirigidos a los astronautas. Estos podrían inhalarse o introducirse en los ojos, causando problemas que pueden ser graves.
Hay alternativas. La propia Estación Espacial Internacional prescinde del vidrio convencional y lo sustituye por vidrios técnicos. Concretamente, para las cristaleras de la cúpula se usan ventanas de sílice fundida y borosilicato, cubiertas con paneles protectores. Estos, a su vez, tienen varias subsecciones: un panel interior antiarañazos, dos paneles de presión de 25 mm de grosor y un panel exterior. Estos, a su vez, están cubiertos por contraventanas de aluminio que protegen el interior de impactos de basura espacial o meteoroides. Los paneles y ventanas se pueden sustituir en bloque, pero es una maniobra compleja, que requiere una caminata espacial.
La solución de Artemis. Actualmente, en la cápsula Orión de las misiones Artemis se usa también sílice fundida para la parte externa de la ventana, aunque la estructura interior es de acrílico. Poco a poco, la NASA se plantea ampliar el uso de este material, ya que es más estable estructuralmente. Incluso se ha visto que, quizás, podría absorber radiación, aunque esto se debe estudiar más a fondo.
En definitiva, es lógico ir cambiando los materiales según avance la ciencia y las expectativas espaciales, pero lo que no deberíamos hacer jamás es eliminar las ventanas. Han demostrado ser una pieza esencial de los viajes al espacio.

articles.title: Control Resonant is Remedy's most successful Steam launch ever
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Following Alan Wake 2's somewhat slow sales momentum, Remedy Entertainment's first major Steam release in six years appears to have sparked solid growth. Control Resonant immediately eclipsed its predecessor's popularity on the platform, opening at the top of the sales chart and remaining in the top 10 days later.
According to SteamDB, the sequel to Remedy Entertainment's award-winning 2019 shooter has quadrupled its predecessor's peak player count on Steam mere days after its September 24 launch. Control Resonant peaked at approximately 42,799 players, compared with 9,193 for Control Ultimate Edition.
Control Resonant launched as Steam's top-selling game and currently sits at number 10, just behind Dressmaker. It has also earned a "Very Positive" rating on Steam as it approaches 4,000 reviews. Upon its initial launch, critics praised its writing, visual design, music, and action sequences.
 – KAMI (@Okami13_) September 24, 2026
Even pirates are considering buying the game. In a Reddit thread announcing that Control Resonant had been cracked, one commenter drew numerous positive reactions after saying they would pay for the game to support Remedy.
Performance on other platforms also appears strong, with Control Resonant ranking among the PlayStation 5's top 10 sellers in 20 different territories. The game's success comes despite launching during a crowded season that included major releases such as Onimusha: Way of the Sword, The Blood of Dawnwalker, and Wolverine.
Things are about to get even more crowded, with The Witcher 3 Remastered, Ace Combat 8, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and Gears of War: E-Day all launching before Grand Theft Auto VI, the industry's most anticipated game in years.
If Control Resonant can maintain its sales momentum on PC, it could contrast sharply with Alan Wake 2, which some have argued was handicapped by its exclusivity to the Epic Games Store. While Alan Wake 2 became Remedy's fastest-selling game soon after its late-2023 launch and reached three million units earlier this year, it took over a year to recoup its costs despite receiving warm reviews.
Remedy's next project is a remake of the first two Max Payne games. Although the company revealed the project, which will combine both entries into one game, in 2022, its launch likely remains years away. In 2024, the company also announced plans to adapt Control and Alan Wake for TV and film, but details about those projects remain scarce.
